title_en: David Blanchett: Why the Years Before Retirement Can Be So Risky
title_zh: David Blanchett：退休前的那几年为何风险如此之高
subtitle_zh: 退休研究专家 David Blanchett 谈退休前后的支取难题、终身收入与「退休风险区」
summary_zh: 本期 Morningstar 播客 The Long View 由 Amy Arnott 与 Ben Johnson 两位主持对话 David Blanchett——Prudential Financial 退休研究主管、PGIM 投资组合经理，同时是 The American College of Financial Services 的财富管理兼职教授。Blanchett 首先修正了自己著名的退休支出微笑曲线（retirement spending smile）：多数家庭的实际支出其实一路下行，更像一条坏笑曲线（smirk），只有少数家庭因生命末期医疗开销而回升；若把这种下行纳入规划，安全提取率（safe withdrawal rate）可从常见的 4% 到 5% 提升到 5% 到 7%。其次，他指出退休人士普遍不愿动用投资组合，终身收入（lifetime income）是最有效的解药，应被视为组合配置决策而非单纯的保险购买，Social Security 福利的现值也该计入家庭资产负债表。第三，他与 Wade Pfau、Michael Finke 的研究显示，序列风险（sequence risk）在余额最大的退休前三年最具杀伤力，因此临近退休不宜过度激进，可以先略保守、再视运气重新评估。最后他还谈到 tontine（联合养老池）、目标日期基金（target date fund）内嵌年金，以及健康与社交联结对退休满意度的影响，甚至调侃狗派比猫派更快乐。本集为退休前后最棘手的支取与配置决策提供了一套可操作的思考框架。

turns.en: The first is to make plan sponsors okay, including it, we've done a lot there with fiduciary, safe harbor, things like that. turns.zh: 真正去激活那个收入利益。我觉得这正是我们今天看到问题所在的地方。但不管怎样，我喜欢的是整个行业对终身收入年金的关注度在提升。所以对我来说，看到这些解决方案在不断演进是很棒的事：即便参与者

turns.zh: 最终可能并没有在 DC 计划的架构里使用那个产品，也许他们只是产生了好奇；而当他们把钱转出计划、或者到了 65 岁的时候，他们会去跟自己的顾问聊这件事。所以对我来说，我喜欢的是对终身收入的高层关注。至于

turns.zh: 我们能不能在 DC 领域解决掉很多这类问题，我认为还要看参与者的实际使用情况。解决方案会不会就是再来一次助推（nudge），一种自动化的、相当于自动加入（auto-enrollment）反向版本的机制？我看到最近有一些研究在讨论自动终身收入（automatic lifetime income）这个想法。

turns.en: So again, like I think it's, you know, when we've we've done surveys on this and just to be clear, like we would never recommend something where it's irrevocable, where we, you know, someone's money is automatically, you know, annuities without any kind of provision to get it back at a certain age.
turns.zh: 我们还是做过相关调查的。而且要说清楚：我们绝不会推荐那种不可撤销的方案，也就是某个人的钱在到了某个年龄时被自动年金化，却没有任何可以拿回来的条款。

turns.en: But right now you have to opt in to the lifetime income benefit. What if it were the reverse? What if when you were completing the enrollment form, whatever else it is, it would say, hey, we're going to assume at age 65, you will start receiving benefits.
turns.zh: 但现在你必须主动选择加入（opt in）才能拿到终身收入利益。如果反过来呢？如果你在填注册表格或者别的东西时，上面写着：嘿，我们将默认你在 65 岁时开始领取福利。

turns.en: I think that would have a meaningful increase in participants that receive the life of a minute. And I think it actually people happier. I think if you see surveys on those that have bought left to lose, they tend to be happy they made a decision. The problem is going to be like pull the trigger.
turns.zh: 我认为这会让实际领取终身年金的参与者人数出现有意义的增长，而且我觉得它实际上会让人更快乐。如果你去看那些买了终身年金的人的调查，他们往往对自己做了这个决定感到满意。问题在于扣动扳机那一步。

turns.en: And so to your point, like the more we can make it automatic, the easier it's going to be to kind of reduce those friction points towards utilization. Well, in part of it might also be education, you know, with plan sponsors trying to educate their employees, you know, maybe starting when people are 55 and just, you know, helping
turns.zh: 所以就像你说的，我们越能把它自动化，就越容易减少走向实际使用过程中的那些摩擦点。嗯，一部分可能也在于教育，比如计划发起人去教育自己的员工，也许从人们 55 岁的时候就开始，帮助他们

Yeah, I mean, I think education can do a lot. I think, you know, people's interest in consuming that and acting upon it just varies dramatically. Right?
turns.zh: 理解自己在退休时有哪些选择，并且在退休之前就此展开持续的沟通和教育努力。是啊，我觉得教育能做很多事。但人们去吸收这些信息并据此行动的意愿，差别真的非常大，对吧？

turns.en: I think advisors are critical. I think advice just is, you know, people, I think benefit from advice to what the life's like, but around retirement is where having access to an advisor or even maybe robot tools or advice can really help someone make the best choices possible.
turns.zh: 我认为顾问是至关重要的。人们在整个生命周期中都能从建议中受益，但正是在退休这个环节，能够接触到一位顾问、甚至是一些智能投顾（robo）工具或建议，才真正能帮助一个人做出尽可能最好的选择。

turns.en: And so I think, yes, like the more we can do to educate people, the better, but retirements really, really, really complicated. And so it's kind of hard to get people kind of up to speed where they probably would need to be to make these decisions on their own without some kind of help.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，是的，我们在教育人们方面做得越多越好，但退休这件事真的、真的、真的很复杂。因此很难把人们提升到那种水平——如果没有某种帮助，他们要独立做出这些决定所需要的水平。

turns.en: You've also done some research on new structures like protected modern tanteens. What problem are tanteens solving that conventional annuities don't solve particularly well? Sure. So there's lots of different ways that you can create mortality pooled structures.
turns.zh: 你还研究过一些新型结构，比如带保护的现代 tontine（联合养老池）。tontine 解决的是传统年金没有解决好的什么问题？好。要构建死亡率池化（mortality pooling）结构有很多种不同的方式。

turns.en: And in the U.S., the, you know, 99.99% of the assets are in solutions that are offered by insurance companies that have an explicit guarantee. Another way to structure it is via what's called a tanteen. And there's, there's also, there's modern tanteens. There's like pooled long.
turns.zh: 在美国，99.99% 的资产都放在由保险公司提供、带有明确保证的解决方案里。另一种构建方式就是通过所谓的 tontine。另外还有现代 tontine（modern tontine），还有池化长寿（pooled longevity）之类的。

turns.en: There's lots of words we can use to describe these, but effectively what they are is a group of individuals get together and the payouts you receive depend upon the mortality experience of that pool, right? And so a benefit there is that the payouts can be higher because there's no kind of insurance
turns.zh: 描述这些东西可以用很多不同的词，但它们本质上就是：一群个人凑在一起，你拿到的给付取决于这个池子的死亡率经验（mortality experience），对吧？这样做的好处是给付可以更高，因为没有保险

turns.en: company charging its fee to minister and guarantee the payouts. The con though is that if that, if that group lives a really long time, your payouts could be lower. And so, you know, we've seen structures introduced in the U.S. and in Canada. There's a lot going on that's very similar in the UK and Australia.
turns.zh: 公司收取费用来管理并保证这些给付。缺点则是，如果那群人活得很长，你拿到的给付可能会变低。我们已经看到这类结构在美国和加拿大被引入，英国和澳大利亚也有很多非常类似的进展。

turns.en: So I do think we're going to see a lot of innovation in this space because the benefits of life to income are pretty powerful. I do believe that having some guarantees is probably really important like out of the gate, especially in the U.S. given the current market environment, but the idea of
turns.zh: 所以我确实认为，我们会在这个领域看到很多创新，因为终身收入的好处是相当强大的。我也确实相信，一开始就有一些保证可能是非常重要的，尤其是在美国、在当前市场环境下。但

turns.en: you know, more structures to create protected lifetime income, I think, is great for retirees. Yeah. And one of the classic problems with tanteens is if you're in a pool with a group of other people and you get more money if someone else dies, obviously that, you know, could create bad incentives or possible, you know, murder plots or...
turns.zh: 用更多结构去创造带保护的终身收入，这个想法我认为对退休人士是好事。是啊。tontine 的一个经典问题是：如果你和一群人同处一个池子，别人死了你能拿到更多钱，那显然可能产生糟糕的激励，甚至可能出现谋杀阴谋之类的……

I mean, I think the key is ensuring a large enough pool, right, you know, like realistically you want thousands and thousands of people. But I think that like that's something that has existed in kind of fictional shows and
turns.zh: 是是是，我们都被问过这个，是是。不过我想确实有办法绕开这个问题，确实有。我认为关键在于确保池子足够大，对吧？现实地说，你会希望有成千上万的人。不过我觉得，那类情节更多是出现在虚构的影视剧里，

And I think we've done a really good job innovating in the, like the guaranteed space.
turns.zh: 也有书写过。但我觉得大体上真正有意思的是这样一种认知：我们面对的是一个减积累难题（decumulation puzzle），而与寿命挂钩的解决方案是解开它的一条路。我认为我们在有保证的这一块已经做了非常出色的创新，

turns.zh: 对我来说那大概是一个正适合创新的领域。借用你的词，David，我们这里谈论的这个难题实在太复杂、也太私人了：从寿命到支出偏好和习惯，形形色色的假设，不一而足。

turns.en: out what their client should spend, you know, I could go, I could spend a lot of time talking about where I think the calculators don't use the best assumptions, but I think like the key behind the calculators is giving and the advisors is giving clients some level of a shirt. Right?
turns.zh: 他们的客户应该花多少钱。我可以花很多时间去讲我认为这些计算器在哪些地方没有采用最好的假设，但我觉得计算器背后、以及顾问背后的关键，是给客户某种程度的确定性（certainty），对吧？

turns.en: If you don't have access to an advisor, if you don't use the calculators, you don't have any idea what you can do. And so, I mean, yes, like, you know, I love to get into the weeds and talk about the nuances of like what you should do for your longevity assumptions and how you model returns and how
turns.zh: 如果你接触不到顾问，也不用这些计算器，你就完全不知道自己该怎么做。所以，是的，我很喜欢钻进细节里去谈那些微妙之处，比如你的寿命假设该怎么设、回报该怎么建模、

But I think like the key is just, is having a plan because the plan gives you peace of mind about what is a reasonable thing to do today. I think that what's really hard right is that if you think about retirement, it could last
turns.zh: 我们如何纳入动态提取（dynamic withdrawals）等等这些不同的东西。但我觉得关键就是：要有一个方案，因为方案能让你对今天做什么才算合理感到安心。我认为真正难的地方在于，如果你想想退休，它可能持续

turns.zh: 30 年或 40 年，而现实是我们只能告诉某个人：截至今天、这个零时刻，他可以怎么做。这也正是它们的价值所在。所以我认为关键在于，规划能给予某个人那种信心，让他真的能享受自己的退休生活；因为缺了这份信心，人们往往就花得非常少。

turns.en: We also wanted to spend some time talking about the retirement risk zone. And I think the conventional wisdom is that five year window after retirement is the riskiest period, but you've actually found the returns immediately before retirement can matter more than returns after you retire. Can you explain why you found that pattern? Sure.
turns.zh: 我们还希望花点时间谈谈退休风险区（retirement risk zone）。我想传统的看法是，退休后的那五年窗口期是风险最高的阶段，但你实际上发现，退休前紧挨着的那段时间的回报，可能比退休后的回报更重要。你能解释一下为什么会出现这种模式吗？好。

turns.en: So that was a piece I did with Wade Fowler, Michael Finca, looking at the idea of sequence risk. And there's lots of ways that you can think about how the returns on a portfolio affect the outcome. And I think that a lot of advisors think that sequence risk is the greatest when you first retire.
turns.zh: 那是我和 Wade Pfau、Michael Finke 一起做的一项研究，考察的是序列风险（sequence risk）这个概念。关于组合回报如何影响最终结果，有很多种思考方式。我认为很多顾问觉得，序列风险在你刚退休的时候最大。

turns.en: But realistically, sequence risk is the greatest when your balance is the largest. And the balance is the largest, like just before you retire in the years before that. And so I think that, you know, one thing that is just really important is not to be overly aggressive as your entering retirement. You can always risk on in retirement.
turns.zh: 但实际上，序列风险最大的时候是你余额最大的时候。而余额最大的时候，就在你退休之前、以及之前的那几年。所以我认为有一件事真的很重要：进入退休时不要过于激进。在退休期间你随时可以再加风险（risk on），

turns.en: What did you choose to do so? But I just wouldn't want someone to think, oh, like sequence risk is really only a big deal when I first retire. I'm going to take on, you know, too much risk three years before retirement and then have this kind of really big market event.
turns.zh: 如果你想这么做的话。我只是不希望有人想：哦，序列风险只有在我刚退休时才是大事，于是在退休前三年承担过多风险，结果碰上一场真正巨大的市场事件。

turns.en: And so the idea is just that like the impact of bad returns, like varies over time, but it really is the most consequential. It's really like the three years leading up to your retirement. What does that mean, David, just with respect to traditional rules of thumb around like de-risking portfolios, is that moment approaches?
turns.zh: 所以这个观点就是：糟糕回报的影响会随时间变化，而真正最有杀伤力的，其实是你退休前的那三年。David，就传统的关于在临近那个时点时给组合降风险（de-risking）的经验法则而言，这意味着什么？

turns.en: I mean, if anything, I'm thinking of a glide path in almost a moment where you kind of like come from 30,000 feet down to 10,000 feet and then turn the nose back up. How does that cause us to maybe potentially rethink just traditional notions of how we dial up or down our portfolio risk, our financial risk, as we come near to retirement?
turns.zh: 我是说，如果非要打个比方，我会想到一条下滑路径（glide path）：你几乎是从 30,000 英尺降到 10,000 英尺，然后再把机头抬起来。这会如何促使我们重新思考传统上关于临近退休时怎样调高或调低组合风险、财务风险的那些观念？

turns.en: Yeah, so I mean, I think what you said is pretty spot on. I mean, if you're at 30,000 feet, you come to 10,000 feet and maybe you could go back up or you land a plane, right? And so I think the key is, I'm not suggesting by any means that you move all into cash and you go crazy and serve because that's risky too.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得你说得相当到位。我是说，如果你从 30,000 英尺降到 10,000 英尺，也许你可以再爬升，或者你就把飞机降落了，对吧？所以我认为关键在于——我绝不是建议你全部转成现金、保守到极点，因为那样也有风险。

turns.en: I think the key is getting through early retirement and seeing how your, I mean, just use the word luck has treated you. If you look back in time, certain retirees have been fantastically lucky. They've experienced market returns that were just explosive, fantastic for the first 10 or 15 years. Others have had the exact opposite.
turns.zh: 我觉得关键是先熬过退休早期，看看——我就直接用运气这个词吧——运气是怎么对待你的。回顾历史，某些退休人士的运气好得惊人，他们在头 10 年或 15 年经历了爆发式、极其出色的市场回报；另一些人的遭遇则恰恰相反。

turns.en: And the thing is, that's out of your hands. You don't know what's going to happen there. And so if you're lucky and then you can possibly risk on, risk on. If you're unlucky and you've got to kind of make hard choices, do that. But for me, the key there is not being overly conservative or aggressive as you move into retirement.
turns.zh: 而问题在于，这不在你的掌控之中，你不知道那时会发生什么。所以如果你运气好，那你也许可以再加风险；如果你运气不好，那就不得不做一些艰难的选择。但对我来说，关键是在你步入退休时，不要过于保守，也不要过于激进。

turns.en: It's probably being maybe a little bit conservative and then reevaluating as your situation evolves. What about the decision of when to retire? You know, I think right now we've had this fantastic bull market that's been almost uninterrupted for such a long time. We have record numbers of 401k millionaires.
turns.zh: 大概是可以稍微保守一点，然后随着情况的变化再重新评估。那么什么时候退休这个决定呢？我想眼下我们经历了这样一场出色的牛市，而且几乎不间断地持续了这么长时间，401(k) 百万富翁的人数创下纪录。

turns.en: So I have to imagine there are a lot of people out there who are looking at their balances and saying, you know, I hit my number, I'm going to retire. But is this potentially a riskier time, you know, because of reversions to the mean, you know, the bull market is not going to last forever.
turns.zh: 所以我只能想象，外面有很多人正看着自己的余额说：我达到我的目标数字了，我要退休了。但这会不会反而是一个风险更高的时点？因为存在均值回归（reversion to the mean），牛市不可能永远持续下去。

turns.en: So yeah, I want it to last forever before I, before I can be on it, I think if the markets could go up 15% a year every year for the next 50 years, that would be absolutely fantastic. But I guess, you know, for anyone that studied history, that hasn't been the case, right?
turns.zh: 是啊，我也希望它能永远持续下去。我想如果市场能在未来 50 年里每年都上涨 15%，那绝对太棒了。但我想，对任何研究过历史的人来说，情况从来不是这样的，对吧？

turns.en: I mean, we've had an exceptional period of just phenomenal performance. And if history is a guide, it is increasingly unlikely to continue. And so I think there's a really unique question people have to ask themselves is, you know, if the markets correct and they go down 30 or 40%, I'm just picking a number, how does
turns.zh: 我是说，我们经历了一段非同寻常的、表现极为惊人的时期。而如果以历史为指南，这种表现越来越不可能延续下去。所以我认为人们必须问自己一个非常独特的问题：如果市场回调、下跌 30% 或 40%——我只是随便挑一个数字——这会

turns.en: that affect your retirement, right? And this is not a suggestion to be tactical, but this is a different environment and that you can invest and fix income today and achieve an incredibly attractive return versus maybe historical long-term averages. And so if you're at the point of retirement and you can retire, you know, how are you
turns.zh: 怎样影响你的退休？对吧？这并不是在建议你去择时（tactical），但今天的环境确实不一样：你现在投资固定收益（fixed income），相比历史上的长期平均水平，能够获得极具吸引力的回报。所以如果你已经到了退休这个节点、也能够退休，你会

turns.en: thinking about investing your portfolio? And I don't want you to go crazy, crazy conservative, but you know, if you keep risking on, if you're all inequities, you're all in large caps, whatever else it is, what would the implications of that be? And I think what we often forget, these unique correlations between, you know, the odds
turns.zh: 怎么考虑自己组合的投资？我不希望你变得极端保守，但如果你继续加风险，如果你全部押在股票上、全部押在大盘股上，或者别的什么，那会带来什么后果？我认为我们常常忘记的是，你被裁员的概率

turns.en: of you getting laid off, for example, and your portfolio, where, you know, if you're two or three years from retirement, you're thinking, man, if I just stay crazy, aggressive for the next two or three years, I'm going to be golden, well, if next week the market drops
turns.zh: 和你的组合之间存在着独特的相关性。举个例子：如果你离退休还有两三年，你会想，伙计，只要我在接下来两三年里保持极度激进，我就稳了。可如果下周市场

turns.en: dramatically, the odds of you getting let go at your job increased dramatically too. So I think, you know, I wouldn't want someone to think that, oh, I'm going to keep being aggressive because the markets have done so well. To your point, it might be time to take risk off the table if a correction really would
turns.zh: 大幅下跌，你在工作上被裁掉的概率也会大幅上升。所以我认为，我不希望有人想：哦，因为市场表现这么好，我就要继续保持激进。就像你说的，如果一次回调真的会

turns.en: affect you, especially if you don't have the capacity to kind of rally from that, right? So if you're younger, it's like, okay, if you're 45 years old, the markets crash, you've still got 20 years to work. If you're 63 years old and, you know, kind of at the tail end of your career, you don't
turns.zh: 影响到你，那也许就该把风险从桌面上撤下来了，尤其是当你没有能力从那种打击中恢复过来的时候，对吧？如果你还年轻，那好吧——如果你 45 岁，市场崩了，你还有 20 年可以工作；但如果你 63 岁、已经处在职业生涯的尾声，你就

turns.en: really have time for that bad luck to correct itself. David, some of the recent research you've done begins to move beyond just like the most immediately measurable versions of wealth and expands that definition a bit looking beyond just to your financial wealth.
turns.zh: 没有那么多时间让那种坏运气自我修正了。David，你最近做的一些研究开始超越那些最直接可度量的财富版本，把这个定义扩展了一些，不只是看你的金融财富。

turns.en: I'm curious, among your findings, what surprised you most about the relationship between that actual measurable wealth I've finished with $10 million, I've reached retirement and how satisfied those retirees actually are or are not. Sure. So at a high level, you know, most Americans are very satisfied in retirement.
turns.zh: 我很好奇，在你的发现当中，最让你意外的是什么——关于那种实际可度量的财富（比如我退休时手上有 1,000 万美元）与这些退休人士实际满意或不满意的程度之间的关系？好。从大的层面看，大多数美国人对退休生活是非常满意的。

turns.en: So the health and retirement study asks this question, like overall, you know, how would you say your satisfactory retirement and the answers are like very moderately not at all. And about half of Americans are very satisfied with retirement. So like collectively, you know, like we're actually doing in fantastic shape, about 85, 90
turns.zh: Health and Retirement Study 会问这样一个问题：总的来说，你会怎么评价你对退休生活的满意度？答案选项是非常满意、中等满意、一点也不满意。大约一半的美国人对退休生活非常满意。所以从整体上看，我们的状态其实非常好：大约 85%、90%

turns.en: percent or either moderately are very satisfied. So collectively, a really happy group. And you know, I focus a lot on like the financial aspects of retirement. So, you know, things like what is your overall level of savings and how much income do you have this guaranteed for life?
turns.zh: 的人属于中等满意或非常满意。所以整体上是一群相当快乐的人。而我关注的很多是退休的财务层面，比如你总体的储蓄水平是多少、你有多少收入是终身有保障的？

turns.en: And those are also both positively correlated to well-being. The more wealth you have, the happier you are, the more life you're thinking about the happier you are. But if you look at other factors, like social connectivity and health, those are probably
turns.zh: 这两者也都与幸福感（well-being）正相关：财富越多，你越快乐；终身收入越多，你也越快乐。但如果你看看其他因素，比如社会联结（social connectivity）和健康，它们可能

turns.en: like even more important in terms of the spectrum of happiness as you move across different levels. And so I think that, you know, this is kind of somewhat out of my domain of expertise. But, you know, like if you get to retirement with lots of money and lots of lifetime income,
turns.zh: 在你跨越不同层级时，对幸福感谱系的影响甚至更为重要。所以我认为——这多少有点超出我的专业领域了——但如果你到了退休时有很多钱、有很多终身收入，

turns.en: but no friends and you're in poor health, you're going to be pretty miserable, right? And that's obvious. But like that's not the kind of things that like I am talking about. And I don't know how often advisors talk about it. But I think to me, the key here is if you look at kind of like what is related to retirement
turns.zh: 却没有朋友、健康状况又很差，你会过得相当痛苦，对吧？这显而易见，但这不是我平时谈的那类东西，我也不知道顾问们多常谈这个。不过对我来说，关键在于：如果你去看什么与退休

turns.en: satisfaction, there's a lot more than just the financial stuff. And that's obvious. But to me, what was surprising in this research, it focuses on this idea of like wealth and well-being, is just how much kind of, how much more important that other stuff.
turns.zh: 满意度相关，那么远不止财务那一块。这显而易见。但对我来说，这项聚焦财富与幸福感（wealth and well-being）这一理念的研究里，令人意外的是，那些别的东西要重要得多。

turns.en: And again, that was health and social connectivity was in terms of defining how happy someone is, especially in retirement. So also along the lines of non-financial factors in retirement, you recently wrote a piece for Kipplinger, titled Dog People versus Cat People, who has a better retirement.
turns.zh: 再强调一次，那就是健康和社会联结——在定义一个人有多快乐、尤其是在退休期间有多快乐方面。那么，同样沿着退休中非财务因素这条线：你最近为 Kiplinger 写了一篇文章，标题是 Dog People versus Cat People: Who Has a Better Retirement（养狗的人 vs 养猫的人：谁的退休生活更好）。

turns.en: So what did you find there and do you think there are any other factors that might be contributing to differences between the two? So before the next, that was like a little bit for fun. So as background, my wife is a veterinarian. We have three dogs, two guinea pigs and a tortoise. And so we're big in the pet game.
turns.zh: 那你在那里发现了什么？你觉得还有没有其他因素可能导致两者之间的差异？先说明一下，那篇多少是写着玩的。背景是这样：我太太是兽医，我们养了三条狗、两只豚鼠和一只陆龟，所以在宠物这件事上我们投入很深。

turns.en: And every year, Prinential does what's called a Pulse Survey. And we included a few questions in the Pulse Survey asking individuals, do you own pets? If so, do you own cats, dogs, cats and dogs or something else? And so I was really curious, how does pet ownership change over time with any kind of relationships
turns.zh: 每年 Prudential 都会做一个叫 Pulse Survey 的调查。我们在这个调查里加了几个问题：你养宠物吗？如果养，你养的是猫、狗、猫和狗，还是别的什么？所以我很好奇，养宠物的情况随时间如何变化，以及它与人生结果之间有没有某种

turns.en: between life outcomes and pet ownerships? One high-level finding was that pet ownership really does decline pretty significantly at older ages. I think that that's somewhat intuitive, right? I think that we have, I didn't want the tortoise. If we're not honest, we're the one with the tortoise.
turns.zh: 关系。一个较高层面的发现是：养宠物的比例在较高年龄段确实会相当显著地下降。我觉得这在某种程度上是符合直觉的，对吧？我是说——那只陆龟不是我想要的；说实话，养陆龟的那个人就是我。

turns.en: And so I think a lot of times we have pets because our kids want them. But as we get older, though, there's a strong relationship between if you have a pet today and you have one when you're retired. Next I looked at things like how life outlook changed across different types of pets.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得很多时候我们养宠物是因为孩子想养。但随着年龄增长，今天你养宠物和退休后你还养宠物之间有很强的关联。接下来我看的是，不同宠物类型之间，人们的生活心态（life outlook）有何变化。

turns.en: And the differences weren't technically statistically significant, but there were differences in that individuals who own dogs had better life outlooks than those who own cats. And so if you own a cat and a dog, you were technically fine because you're also a dog owner.
turns.zh: 严格来说这些差异并没有达到统计显著，但确实存在差异：养狗的人比养猫的人有更好的人生心态。所以如果你既养猫又养狗，严格来说你没问题，因为你同时也是养狗的人。

turns.en: But there was this difference in how people perceive their retirement changing. And part of that could just be because people that own cats are different and those that own dogs, but as someone who was on team dog, I was delighted to see that team dog folks tend to be a bit happier than the team cat folks.
turns.zh: 但人们对于自己退休生活会如何变化，确实存在这样的感知差异。其中一部分原因可能只是养猫的人和养狗的人本身就不一样。但作为一个狗派（team dog）的人，我很高兴地看到，狗派的人往往比猫派的人更快乐一些。

turns.en: Well, and of course, if you own a dog, you have to take your dog for walks. So you're getting exercise, you're going out and meeting people. So I think that actually a huge part of it is that like, you know, I mean, you can just let them outside technically too.
turns.zh: 嗯，当然，如果你养狗，你就得遛狗，所以你得到了锻炼，也出门和人打交道。所以我觉得这实际上是很重要的一部分——我是说，虽然技术上你也可以只是把狗放到外面去。

turns.en: But like it's a more social creature that requires you to engage more in retirement, right? So, you know, like the earlier thing we talked about like with like wealth and well-being. So like, I was thinking about like what are the things that older Americans should do? Like pickleball is a really good example of an activity
turns.zh: 但狗是一种更具社交性的动物，它要求你在退休后有更多的参与，对吧？这就像我们前面谈到的财富与幸福感。所以我就在想，年长的美国人应该做些什么？匹克球（pickleball）就是一个非常好的例子，

turns.en: that addresses both physical health and social connectivity, right? And so having a dog to some extent also kind of addresses both. If you take them on walks, but I think the key is like as we get older, right? Doing things that kind of make us be active and make us see other people
turns.zh: 它同时兼顾了身体健康和社会联结，对吧？所以从某种意义上说，养一条狗也同时兼顾了这两点——如果你带它去散步的话。但我觉得关键在于：随着我们变老，去做那些能让我们保持活跃、能让我们见到其他人的事情，

turns.en: just because it really does appear to draw a retirement satisfaction. We've got two dogs in our house, David. So I'm just going to put a stamp of statistical significance on your findings. All right, extra side of a confirmation by us on my part. I'm curious when you describe, you know, some of these defining sort of wealth
turns.zh: 因为这确实看起来能提升退休满意度。David，我们家养了两条狗，所以我准备给你的发现盖上一个统计显著的章。好，那我这边的确认又多了一份数据点。我很好奇，当你描述这些把财富

turns.en: more broadly concepts.
turns.zh: 定义得更宽泛的概念时，

turns.en: How do you think about advisors role and engaging with clients in things that like aren't showing up on a quarterly statement or in a spreadsheet? Have you seen, you know, any advisors kind of expand into these corners, things that they might be doing successfully or less so? I mean, I'd like to think so.
turns.zh: 你怎么看待顾问的角色——在那些不会出现在季度对账单或电子表格里的事情上与客户互动？你有没有看到一些顾问在往这些角落延伸，他们做得成功的、或者不太成功的？嗯，我愿意相信是有的。

turns.en: I think that a lot of advisors might view their role as wealth maximizers, right? It's my job to build a really efficient portfolio and pick these fantastic investments. And that will allow my client to achieve their goals and objectives. And I wouldn't say that that's wrong, but that's not the whole story, right?
turns.zh: 我觉得很多顾问可能把自己的角色看作财富最大化者，对吧？我的工作是构建一个非常高效的组合、挑选那些出色的投资，这样我的客户就能实现他们的目标。我不会说这是错的，但这不是故事的全部，对吧？

turns.en: It's this idea of, you know, your client can have a gigantic portfolio, but if they're not spending money on things they would enjoy because they're fixated on that portfolio, then you're not helping your client achieve the best possible retirement. And so I think that it does require maybe a different type of conversation
turns.zh: 就是说，你的客户可能拥有一个巨大的组合，但如果他们因为死死盯着那个组合，而不去把钱花在自己真正享受的事情上，那你就没有帮助客户实现最好的退休生活。所以我认为，这确实需要一种不同类型的对话，

turns.en: than this pure investment focused outcomes analysis. Because, you know, if your client gets to retirement and gets to retirement and you just grow the portfolio and they don't enjoy it, that to me isn't the optimal outcome. But I do think more advisors are kind of hyper aware of this, but, you know,
turns.zh: 而不只是那种纯粹以投资为中心的结果分析。因为如果你的客户到了退休、真的退休了，而你只是把组合做大了，他们却没有享受，那在我看来不是最优结果。不过我确实认为，越来越多的顾问对此高度警觉，但你知道，

turns.en: I'll be, this isn't my domain of expertise. You know, I don't know how to have the conversations with people about the importance of health, the importance of social connectivity. But, you know, like one of the things that, you know, that another researcher found recently
turns.zh: 坦白说，这不是我的专业领域。我不知道该怎么和人去谈健康的重要性、社会联结的重要性。但最近另一位研究者发现的一点是，

turns.en: is that like, there's like a positive correlation between how long you live and, you know, having lifetime income. And I think the first thing you have to acknowledge there is that people that are healthier are much more likely to buy or allocate to lifetime income.
turns.zh: 寿命长短与拥有终身收入之间存在正相关。我觉得首先必须承认的是：更健康的人更有可能去购买或配置终身收入产品。

turns.en: There's indogeneity like, of course, people that that have lifetime income, you know, by definition, they tend to be healthy in the average American. So let's just assume we can control for that. I think there's this spillover effect there where, you know, if you have it and you have money, you can spend money on things that you enjoy.
turns.zh: 这里存在内生性（endogeneity）：当然，拥有终身收入的人，从定义上讲往往比一般美国人更健康。那我们就假设可以把这一点控制掉。我认为这里存在一种溢出效应（spillover effect）：如果你有保障、也有钱，你就会把钱花在自己享受的事情上。

turns.en: You will go on vacations, you will do things with it that do have positive long-term outcomes. And like, you can't, you're not going to see that in a mean variance optimization, right? There are things that kind of exist beyond how we think about investments and proving outcome
turns.zh: 你会去度假，你会用它去做一些确实带来积极长期结果的事情。而这些，你在均值—方差优化（mean-variance optimization）里是看不到的，对吧？有些东西存在于我们思考投资、改善结果的方式之外，

turns.en: that really can matter for retirement that I think advisors should hopefully just think more about when it comes to creating these plans for the clients. You can feel confident when you go to buy that new golden doodle or whatever it is. I mean, like, so again, like, I mean, like, tongue and cheek, I mentioned pickleball,
turns.zh: 而它们对退休真的可能很重要。我希望顾问在为客户制定这些方案时能多想一想这些。这样你去买那只新的金贵犬（goldendoodle）或者别的什么的时候，心里也会更有底。我是说，所以再说一次——我提到匹克球是半开玩笑的，

turns.en: but I think like, that's a great example. You know, like, you know, to the extent that you allow yourself to enjoy that, and I don't know, go on trips or do things, like, that can have a meaningful impact on retirement satisfaction. There's this question, like, do you think you can afford to do it, right?
turns.zh: 但我觉得那是个很好的例子。如果你允许自己去享受它，去旅行、去做些事情，那能对退休满意度产生有意义的影响。这里就有个问题：你觉得自己负担得起吗，对吧？

turns.en: And if you convince yourself that you can't afford to take these vacations and these things you love, I think they can have really important negative long term implications on your retirement satisfaction.
turns.zh: 如果你说服自己负担不起这些假期、这些你热爱的事情，我认为这会对你的退休满意度产生非常重要的负面长期影响。

turns.en: Before we wrap up, I wanted to ask if you could kind of redesign the standard retirement planning process from scratch based on what you've learned in your research. What are the main assumptions you would change first? So, you know, people kind of talk longingly about define benefit plans, right?
turns.zh: 在结束之前，我想问一下：如果让你根据自己在研究中学到的东西，从零开始重新设计标准的退休规划流程，你会最先改掉哪些主要假设？人们总是带着怀念谈论固定收益型养老金计划（defined benefit plans），对吧？

turns.en: There's this kind of, you know, I mean, we, and you could argue, like the healthy on days of when people had pensions, I mean, good old days. You know, we still have, we still have so security, okay? And I do not think define benefit plans really make a ton of sense for most companies today. Like, you, like, you, you build widgets.
turns.zh: 你会听到有人说当年大家都有养老金的好日子——我是说，那种怀旧的说法。要知道，我们现在还有 Social Security，好吗？而且我并不认为固定收益型计划对今天大多数公司来说真的很有道理。比如说，你是做小部件（widgets）的，

turns.en: Like, why do you want to have to hire someone who is, like, 45, and they work for you for 10 years, and then in 10 years, you've got to start, like, it, it doesn't make sense for companies to be doing this, but like, that's for, like, insurance companies or other pulled products exist.
turns.zh: 你为什么想要雇一个 45 岁的人，让他为你工作 10 年，然后 10 年后你就得开始给付？这对公司来说是不合理的。但这就是保险公司或者其他池化（pooled）产品存在的意义。

turns.en: And so, I think that, I think the defined contribution space is very much here to stay. But I really do wish there was this, you know, bigger focus on just converting savings to lifetime income when you retire, because it just radically simplifies everything. We've created a situation we've got 100 million-ish households at some point
turns.zh: 所以我认为缴费确定型（defined contribution）这一块是肯定会留下来的。但我真的希望，大家能更关注一件事：在退休时把储蓄转化为终身收入，因为它能极大简化一切。我们造成了这样一种局面：大约有 1 亿户家庭在某个时点

turns.en: have to figure this out on their own. And the evidence from other countries in our own just suggests that, that we're not good at that. And so, I think the more that, you know, I don't, I don't want to use this word, mandates, but like, the more that we can kind of refocus,
